(a) Repeal of Prohibition on Payment of Interest on Demand Deposits.—
        (1) Federal reserve act.—Section 19(i) of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371a) is amended to read as follows:“(i) 
[Repealed]”
. 
        (2) Home owners’ loan act.—The first sentence of section 5(b)(1)(B) of the Home Owners’ Loan Act (12 U.S.C. 1464(b)(1)(B)) is amended by striking “savings association may not—” and all that follows through “(ii) permit any” and inserting “savings association may not permit any”. 
        (3) Federal deposit insurance act.—Section 18(g) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1828(g)) is amended to read as follows:“(g) 
[Repealed]”
.  
    (b) Effective Date.—The amendments made by subsection (a) shall take effect 1 year after the date of the enactment of this Act.

fable.w: This section only repeals statutory prohibitions on paying interest on demand deposits and sets an effective date one year after enactment. It contains no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking grant, or right to sue involving any party outside the federal government. A reader might be tempted to infer rulemaking because banking regulation is involved, but the text simply amends the statutes directly and delegates nothing.

opus.w: The section repeals the statutory ban on paying interest on demand deposits and sets an effective date one year after enactment. It does not require or authorize rulemaking, comment periods, hearings, advisory bodies, consultation with outside parties, or a right to sue. The repealed provisions may once have involved regulations, but repealing them adds no participation; if anything, it removes regulatory authority.

opus.b: **Label: No.** The tempting reading is that the repealed provisions, Federal Reserve Act §19(i) and FDIA §18(g), used to involve federal rulemaking on deposit interest. So touching them might look like rulemaking authority. That reading fails: this section only repeals them and sets an effective date. It grants no rulemaking authority and creates no outside-party process.

qwen_chat.w: This section repeals statutory prohibitions on paying interest on demand deposits. It does not establish any process for public comment, consultation with outside entities, or advisory committees. The change is a direct legislative amendment without a mandated participatory mechanism for the government's decision-making process regarding the repeal itself.
qwen_chat.s: (a) Repeal of Prohibition on Payment of Interest on Demand Deposits.— (1) Federal reserve act.—Section 19(i) of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 371a) is amended to read as follows:“(i) [Repealed]” . (2) Home owners’ loan act.—The first sentence of section 5(b)(1)(B) of the Home Owners’ Loan Act (12 U.S.C. 1464(b)(1)(B)) is amended by striking “savings association may not—” and all that follows through “(ii) permit any” and inserting “savings association may not permit any”. (3) Federal deposit insurance act.—Section 18(g) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (12 U.S.C. 1828(g)) is amended to read as follows:“(g) [Repealed]” . (b) Effective Date.—The amendments made by subsection (a) shall take effect 1 year after the date of the enactment of this Act.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that repealing a prohibition allows banks to set interest rates based on market forces, which involves customers. However, the text itself does not mandate any consultation, hearing, or participation process; it simply changes the legal status of interest payments. The definition requires the government to consult or coordinate with outsiders *before* making a decision. Here, the "decision" is the legislative repeal, and the text does not describe a participatory process for that repeal.
